name: ADUM1200BRZ-RL7
title: ADuM1200/ADuM1201: dual-channel transformer-coupled digital isolators, 2500 V rms, SOIC-8
summary: Two-channel digital isolators that pass logic signals across a 2500 V rms barrier through on-chip transformers. The ADuM1200 sends both channels from side 1 to side 2; the ADuM1201 sends one each way. Each side runs from 2.7 V to 5.5 V, so the part translates between 3 V and 5 V logic. Grades A, B and C reach 1, 10 and 25 Mbps at up to 105 °C; the automotive W grades (WS, WT, WU) match them to 125 °C. A refresh scheme keeps the outputs correct at DC and after power-up.
key_figures: 2.7 V to 5.5 V each side (W grades 3.0 V to 5.5 V)
per channel max: 1.1 mA (0–2 Mbps), 3.7 mA (10 Mbps), 8.2 mA (25 Mbps) at 5 V; 0.8, 2.2, 4.8 mA at 3 V
2500 V rms 1 min (UL 1577); VIORM 560 V peak

notes: Z: RoHS compliant. W: qualified for automotive applications. R-8: 8-lead narrow-body SOIC_N.

operation.text: Each channel carries a logic level across the isolation barrier through an on-chip transformer, with CMOS encode and decode circuits on the two sides; there are no LEDs or photodiodes. Each side runs from its own 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply (3.0 V to 5.5 V for the W grades), so the part also shifts logic levels between a 3 V side and a 5 V side.
ADuM1200: both channels run from side 1 to side 2. ADuM1201: channel B runs from side 1 to side 2 and channel A from side 2 to side 1, one channel each way.

A grade: 1 Mbps, 150 ns propagation delay, 40 ns pulse width distortion. B grade: 10 Mbps, 50 ns, 3 ns. C grade: 25 Mbps, 45 ns, 3 ns (delays at 5 V, maximum). The automotive WS, WT and WU grades match A, B and C and run to 125 °C. Z marks a RoHS-compliant part and W an automotive-qualified part; R-8 is the 8-lead narrow SOIC.

No external parts are needed at the logic pins. Each supply pin, VDD1 and VDD2, gets a bypass capacitor of 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF; the leads from both capacitor ends to the supply pin total no more than 20 mm. The AN-1109 application note covers board layout.

Propagation delay to a low output (tPHL) can differ from that to a high output (tPLH); pulse width distortion is the largest difference between the two and shows how well input timing is kept. Channel-to-channel matching is the largest delay difference between channels in one part; propagation delay skew is the largest delay difference between separate parts under the same conditions. Delays are taken between the 50% points of input and output edges.

Each input edge sends a pulse of about 1 ns through the transformer to a bistable decoder, which sets or resets on it. When the input has not changed for more than about 1 µs, the input side sends refresh pulses that carry the present input state, so the output stays right at DC. If the decoder sees no pulses for more than about 5 µs it takes the input side to be unpowered or faulty, and a watchdog forces the output to its default state (truth tables).

With the input-side supply off and the output side powered, ADuM1200 outputs go high; on the ADuM1201 the outputs on the powered side go high. Outputs on an unpowered side are indeterminate. Outputs follow the inputs again within 1 µs of the missing supply returning.

A field can upset the part only by inducing enough voltage in a receiving coil to set or reset the decoder falsely. At 3 V, the worst case, pulses at the transformer output exceed 1.0 V and the decoder threshold is about 0.5 V, leaving 0.5 V of margin; the maximum allowable flux density curve holds the induced voltage to half that margin. At 1 MHz the limit is 0.2 kgauss, which induces 0.25 V, and a worst-case field arriving during a pulse lowers it from over 1.0 V to 0.75 V. The maximum allowable current curve gives the same limit as current at a distance: at 1 MHz, 0.5 kA flowing 5 mm from the part. Strong fast fields can also induce error voltages in loops formed by board traces, which can trip the circuits that follow.

A channel's supply current depends on supply voltage, data rate and output load. Each input and output channel's current is found from the equations and summed per supply to give IDD1 and IDD2. Typical curves give per-channel current against data rate unloaded and with 15 pF, and the per-supply totals for each model.

Insulation wears out under long voltage stress, at a rate set by the waveform across it: bipolar AC is the hardest case, unipolar AC and DC much milder. Accelerated life tests above the rated working voltage give acceleration factors from which time to failure at the actual working voltage is calculated. The bipolar AC limit (565 V peak) is set for a 50-year life. A waveform that swings between 0 V and a limit of one polarity without crossing 0 V counts as unipolar AC, and a steady voltage as DC; both may run at the higher approved working voltages for 50 years. Any other waveform is treated as bipolar AC and kept to the 50-year bipolar value. Running at an approved working voltage above the 50-year value can shorten insulation life.

The ADuM1200W and ADuM1201W are made under controlled manufacturing for automotive use, are specified in their own 125 °C tables and can differ from the commercial grades. Only the W models are for automotive applications.
